title: The Chan Dharma of Dahui
author: Compiled by Zhanran
excerpt: When the mind has nowhere to go, a mouse entering a cow's horn, then at last the knot is cut through.

inline.s: First, never take hold of it at the very place where it is raised.
Nor must you reason or conjecture about it.
But with whole attention, think right at the place where thought cannot reach.
When the mind has nowhere to go, a mouse entering a cow's horn, then at last the knot is cut through.

Chan practice in our land has a history of more than a thousand years, and its concrete methods are manifold and richly varied. This essay introduces the Chan teaching of Dahui: to raise the single word 'Wu.'
Great Master Dahui Zonggao (
gǎo
): A brief introduction.
A monk of the Yangqi branch of the Linji school in the Song dynasty (

). His style name was Tanhui, his sobriquets Miaoxi and Yunmen. His lay surname was Xi, and he was a native of Ningguo in Xuanzhou (today's Anhui). At seventeen he left home under Huiqi at Huiyun Temple on Mount Dong; the very next (
yì

, 'next, the second') year he received the full precepts. He successively visited such teachers as Dongshan Wei, Zhantang Wenzhun, and Yuanwu Keqin (yuan, the same as 'circle'). During the Xuanhe era he resided with Yuanwu Keqin in the Eastern Capital (Kaifeng); after his great awakening he inherited Yuanwu's Dharma, and Yuanwu entrusted him with the work he had written, the 'Record of the Authentic Linji School.' Before long the master was asked to take the seat and preach in his own right, whereupon the whole community held him in high regard and his fame shook the capital. In the first year of Jingkang (
), Chancellor Lü Shuntu petitioned that the purple robe be bestowed on him, and he received the honorary title 'Great Master Buddha-Sun.' In the seventh year of Shaoxing (
), at the request of Chancellor Zhang Jun, he became abbot of Nengren Temple on Mount Jingshan, and monks and laypeople from all quarters gathered there, and the ancestral style was greatly revived.

In the eleventh year of Shaoxing, Vice Minister Zhang Jiucheng came to Nengren Temple to study Chan with the master and happened to discuss state affairs. At that time Qin Hui held power and pressed hard for peace with the Jurchens, while Zhang Jiucheng belonged to the war party at court. Qin Hui, wielding great authority, did his utmost to root out dissenters, and the master too did not escape, being stripped in the fifth month of that eleventh year (
chǐ

, 'to strip, to deprive') of his robe and ordination documents, and exiled to Hengzhou (present-day Hengyang, Hunan). During this period he collected the striking words of the ancient worthies and the recorded dialogues and gongans he had examined with his disciples, compiling them into the six-juan 'Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.' In the twentieth year of Shaoxing he was further banished to Meizhou (present-day Meizhou, Guangdong), a land of pestilence and barren soil, where more than half of the hundred-odd masters and disciples died; yet the master still conducted himself by the ordinary Way and serenely transformed the local people. In the twenty-fifth year of Shaoxing he received amnesty, and the next year he resumed the monk's robe.

In the twenty-eighth year, by imperial decree he returned to reside at Mount Jingshan, and monastics and laypeople flocked after him as before; at that time he was called 'Dahui Zonggao of Jingshan.' The master's eloquence ranged freely, and in daily life he devoted himself to promulgating the Dharma of gongans, a style that came to be called 'Kanhua Chan' and that shone alongside the 'Mozhao Chan' of Hongzhi Zhengjue. In his later years he dwelt at Jingshan, and monastics and layfolk from the four quarters gathered at the sound of his teaching, with several thousand constantly in his assembly. Emperor Xiaozong took refuge in him and bestowed on him the title 'Great Master Dahui.' In the first year of Longxing (

), in the eighth month he felt slightly unwell; on the tenth day he wrote out his final memorial in his own hand and also a death verse, then cast down the brush and passed into stillness, aged seventy-five, with fifty-eight rainy seasons in the Dharma. His posthumous title was 'Great Master Pujue.' He left behind the Recorded Sayings of Dahui, the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the Dahui Armory, and other works.

[Kanhua Chan] is the ancestral style of Dahui Zonggao of the Linji school. 'Kan' means to see; 'hua' refers to the gongan. That is, taking up a single ancient master's huatou and, through long and real investigation, finally attaining awakening; this style of Chan is called Kanhua Chan. The origin of Kanhua Chan may be traced to Zhaozhou Congshen's 'A dog has no Buddha-nature' in the Tang dynasty, and in the late Tang and the Five Dynasties the custom of raising old gongans to shatter intellectual and emotional discrimination flourished greatly. By the Song, Dahui Zonggao advocated especially investigating a single huatou, and the later Linji school all honored this as its standard. Thereafter this style grew ever more widespread; in the Ming, for example, Zhongfeng Mingben so championed the ancient gongans of 'three catties of hemp,' 'the cypress tree in the courtyard,' 'Mount Sumeru,' 'the ordinary mind is the Way,' 'Yunmen's gu,' and 'Zhaozhou's wu,' profoundly influencing the Chan style of his age. From the Ming and Qing up to the present this style has never died out. Moreover, after the Song the trend of combining Chan and Pure Land practice flourished greatly, and the practice of using the four characters 'Amitabha Buddha' as a gongan was much in vogue for a time; this too is a kind of Kanhua Chan. [Gui nie (
guī niè

)] Refers to the gnomon, used metaphorically for a norm or standard. [Gui biao] Is an astronomical instrument of ancient China, in which a ruler (the gnomon shadow template) is laid flat on a stone base, with a vertical pole (the gnomon) erected at each of its southern and northern ends. By the change in the sun's shadow one can determine the solar terms and the lengths of the seasons and of the year.
To be wholly free of the world's dust is no common feat; grip the rope's end and give it a bout;
Unless you have been chilled through to the very bone, how could the plum blossom's fragrance greet you?
The Tang-era ancestral master Huangbo, in his 'Essentials of the Transmission of Mind,' first opened the way for Kanhua Chan.
[A forerunner] The 'Book of Rites

Record of Learning' says: 'When the three kings sacrificed to the rivers, they first sacrificed to the Yellow River and then to the sea.' The ancients considered the Yellow River the source of the sea, so when the sovereigns offered sacrifice they first sacrificed to the Yellow River and then to the sea. Later the term 'forerunner' came to be used for the first to initiate a thing.
The ancestral master Huangbo admonished the assembly, saying:
'If beforehand you have not seen it through thoroughly
(if you have not prepared well in advance)
, when the night of the last day of the twelfth month arrives
(a metaphor for the end of life, the moment of dying)
, you are sure to be in a frantic flurry
(you will surely be in a panic, all at sixes and sevens)
There are some followers of outside ways who, the moment they hear someone speak of doing practice, sneer: 'You still have
(this)
thing!' Now I ask you
(you)
: when suddenly the hour of your end comes,
with what will you oppose birth and death?
Just you consider it, for there is a principle in it. Where
(which)
would there be a Maitreya born of heaven, or a Sakyamuni come by nature?'
There is a sort of idle ghosts and wild spirits who, the moment they see a person slightly ill, tell him: 'Just let it go.' But when they themselves fall ill they cannot deal with it
(handle, cope with)
at all
(cannot get through it)
, and are all in a fluster; how can they
(what can one do)

help it when their flesh is cut to pieces by a sharp knife and they cannot be masters of themselves? In all matters, one must see it through in time of peace so that it serves one in time of haste; how much saving of effort! Do not wait until you are thirsty to dig the well, when nothing can be done and the whole scene lies in ruins; how could you evade it? The road ahead is dark, and if one believes
(surely)
one will bore and stumble blindly. What misery! What misery! One who in daily life has learned only a lip-service samadhi
(one who in daily life has only learned a verbal samadhi)
, talking of Chan and the Way, reviling the Buddhas and scolding the patriarchs, finds it all of no use here. In daily life he only deceives
others
(one who in daily life simply uses a verbal samadhi to fool others)
, and how
(how)
was he to know that today
(the moment of death)
he has deceived himself?
(this verbal samadhi has deceived even himself, too)
. In the Avici hell, they will certainly not let you go.'
But if you are a true man, a hero
(one who will make something of himself)

, then investigate a gongan. A monk asked Zhaozhou: 'Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?' Zhaozhou said, 'Wu.' Just, all within the twenty-four hours, investigate the word 'Wu.' Investigate by day, investigate by night, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, whether putting on clothes or eating, whether relieving yourself, with the mind intent on it, with fierce spirit
(shaking yourself awake)

: guard the word 'Wu.' As the days and months deepen and it all becomes one mass, suddenly the flower of the mind bursts open, you awaken to the living intent of the Buddhas and patriarchs, and you are no longer deceived by the tongues of all the old monks under heaven, and you can open your mouth wide and say: 'Bodhidharma came from the West and raised waves where there was no wind; the World-Honored One twirled the flower, and it was a failure all round.' At this point, what is all this talk of Old King Yama? Even a thousand sages can do nothing with you! Do you not believe it? Truly
(truly)
there is
(this)

a wonder as this? Why is it so? Affairs yield to the man of resolution! The verse says: To be wholly free of the world's dust is no common feat; grip the rope's end and give it a bout; unless you are chilled through to the very bone, how could the plum blossom's fragrance greet you?'

[Jingcai] Means here 'spirit, vigor.' [Chenlao] The mind wearying in the dust of sense-objects is another name for affliction. [Chenlao jiong tuo shi feichang] To be wholly released from the afflictions (to cut off the delusions of views and of thought) is no ordinary matter. [Jin ba shengtou zuo yi chang] This uses the metaphor of herding an ox: to grip tightly the nose-rope and so tend the mind-ox, and the nose-rope is the huatou 'Wu.' As soon as the huatou is lost, the mind-ox runs wild, even trampling the crops; therefore one must 'grip the rope's end and give it a bout'
, until the ox is tamed and the herdsman at ease, until at last man and ox are both forgotten.
Now let me annotate this single gongan, 'Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?', as follows:
[A monk asked: 'Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?' Zhaozhou said: 'Wu.']
A monk asked, 'Does a dog also have Buddha-nature?' Zhaozhou replied, 'Wu.'

Zhaozhou said: Wu.' This word 'Wu' is the 'Wu' of 'fundamentally there is not a single thing,' and is given in answer on the level of the real nature of all dharmas. In terms of the real nature, not a single dharma exists, and the dog is naturally no exception. If the dog itself does not exist, then how can one speak of whether it has Buddha-nature? The 'Wu' of ordinary speech is a non-being opposed to being; for example, an ox has horns and a rabbit has no horns. This belongs to the dream of ignorance. The 'Wu' of Zhaozhou is a Wu that transcends being and non-being, the 'thing' of 'fundamentally there is not a single thing,' the real nature of all dharmas.
[The dream of ignorance] The Sutra of the Inconceivable State of the Tathagata says:
'All Tathagatas, relying on this samadhi, accomplish immeasurable great spiritual power and even realize the emptiness of all dharmas
(all dharmas are but illusions)

, and can, in all the buddha-lands of the ten directions, display all manner of sovereign deeds. For example, a person dreams of many kinds of transformations, and on waking sees that none of them exist. Ordinary beings likewise, because of the dream of ignorance, falsely conceive of dharmas as real entities. The Buddhas, having awakened, cling to nothing; therefore in all the worlds of the ten directions, in a single thought they display immeasurable buddha-deeds, sovereign and unobstructed, benefiting and perfecting all beings, causing them all to realize and enter the immeasurable, profound, and subtle gate of liberation.'
[The real nature of dharmas] The 'real nature of dharmas' is the actual state of all dharmas. The Buddha-Treasury Sutra says:
'What is called the real nature of dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without any existence.'
The Great Parinirvana Sutra says:
'All dharmas are like illusory forms; the Tathagata, abiding within them by the power of skillful means, is not defiled by them.'
The Lotus Sutra says:
'The bodhisattva mahasattva contemplates that all dharmas are empty, and such is the real nature: without inversion, without movement, without regression, without turning.'
For more discussion of the real nature of dharmas, see this institute's course text
Selected Annotations to the Buddha-Treasury Sutra
Think the unthinkable,'
Or, 'think right where there is nothing to think.'
This is the very marrow of Chan practice: when thinking is exhausted and one returns to the source, one sees the true Buddha.
In the Song dynasty, the ancestral master Dahui earnestly advocated Kanhua Chan and revived the Chan school. Although the huatou may be many, he especially urged raising the single word 'Wu.'
Dahui said:

A thousand doubts and ten thousand doubts are but one doubt. When the doubt on the huatou is broken, then a thousand and ten thousand doubts are broken at once; if the huatou is not broken, then just keep grappling
(holding on, enduring)

with it. If you abandon the huatou and instead raise doubt over other written words, over the teachings, over the gongans of the ancients, or amid the daily dust of toil, all these are the retinue of devils. First, never take hold at the place where the word is raised, and never reason or conjecture about it,
but with whole attention think right where nothing can be thought,
the mind having nowhere to go, like a mouse entering a cow's horn
(only forward, never back)
, and then you will see the knot cut through
(then you see the conclusion, that is, you see the nature and awaken the mind)
. Further, if the square inch
(the mind)

is restless, just raise the case of 'a dog has no Buddha-nature.' The words of the Buddhas, the words of the patriarchs, the words of the old masters everywhere differ in a thousand ways, but if you penetrate the word 'Wu,' you pass through them all at once
(instantly pass through everything)
, and need not ask anyone
(there is no need to ask others)
. If you always
(if you constantly)
ask others how the Buddha's words are, how the patriarchs' words are, how the old masters' words are, then through endless eons you will never have a moment of awakening.'
(From the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dahui Pujue)

[If the huatou is not broken, then just keep grappling with it.] If the doubt on the huatou has not yet broken through, use the huatou to withstand the various delusions (the thousand and ten thousand doubts) and hold on. [Si ai (a-i)] Means to withstand, to endure and get through.
[Lao su] A senior and experienced person; in the Chan school it refers to a venerable, mature elder of virtue.

In this discourse, the ancestral master Dahui not only sets forth the importance of raising the 'Wu' huatou (if you penetrate the word 'Wu', you instantly pass through everything), but also explains the method of raising the 'Wu':

'First, never take hold at the place where the word is raised; nor must you reason or conjecture about it; but with whole attention think right where nothing can be thought, the mind having nowhere to go.'
This passage has three key points:
First, '
never take hold at the place where the word is raised
', that is to say, do not concentrate your mental effort on the very thought of the word 'Wu.' The ancestral master Dahui said:
'Just look at the huatou right here. A monk asked Zhaozhou: 'Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?' Zhaozhou said, 'Wu.' When you look, do not
(do not)
reason it out
(weigh it up)

, do not annotate it, do not want to get an explanation, do not take hold at the place of speech, do not make a principle out of the raising of the word, do not fall into emptiness and stillness, do not hold the mind waiting for awakening, do not comprehend at the place where the master speaks, do not sink into the shell of non-affair.'
Second, '
nor must you reason or conjecture about it
', that is to say, do not go reasoning or conjecturing about what 'Wu' is. Great Master Hanshan said:
'The ancients said: 'The huatou is like a tile used to knock at the door; you knock only to open the door and see the person in the house
(one's true nature)
, not to busy yourself outside the door.' From this it is clear that the doubt which arises by relying on the huatou does not lie in the huatou itself, but must be in the very bottom of one's being.'
(From the Mengyou ji, 'Essential Points on Practicing Chan') He also said:

'Biting down on the huatou is not in order to understand the huatou; you only borrow the huatou to stir up doubt and cut off delusions. Your investigation must proceed from a place beyond the huatou; only when doubt has arisen will it take effect.'
(From the Mengyou ji, 'Miscellaneous Sayings at Jingshan') He further said:
'All this above
(these words above)

is the customary hammer and tongs the old man Dahui used, and its intent is only to have you use the huatou to dam up the flowing stream of delusion beneath the root of conscious intent, and right where it no longer flows, to look upon your original face. It does not teach you to reflect upon the gongan, treating it as a matter of doubt, to seek an explanation.'
(From the Mengyou ji, 'Essential Points on Practicing Chan')
Third, '
but with whole attention think right where nothing can be thought, the mind having nowhere to go

'. This very line is the essence of Chan practice, and is Dahui's instruction to students on how to raise the huatou! 'The mind having nowhere to go' means do not let the mind run off anywhere else. In this way one abides in the thought-free state in which delusions are stilled. The essential point of this method is:
with whole attention
(simply gathering the mind's power)
, think right where nothing can be thought
(to think at the place where thought cannot reach)
. With this formless sense of doubt, pressing hard and bearing down, when thinking is exhausted and one returns to the source, one sees the true Buddha.
Q: How does one 'think at the place where thought cannot reach'?
A: It is very difficult to explain in words; the following gongan can help us enter this state.
'A monk asked: 'What does he ponder so intently
(so earnestly, without cease)
?' The master
(the Chan master Yaoshan Weiyan)
said, '
I think the unthinkable
(thinking the unthinkable)
.' The monk asked: 'How does one think the unthinkable?' The master said: 'By not-thinking.'
(From the Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp
the chapter on Yaoshan Weiyan')
Q: This gongan is hard to understand; please explain it in detail.

A: To the student's question, 'How does one think the unthinkable?', the Chan master Yaoshan Weiyan answered, 'By not-thinking.' That is to say, this thinking is not the kind of thinking carried on with language, written words, concepts, reasoning, or association, but is a 'thinking' that transcends speech and thought, a thinking that is no-thinking.
The Compendium of the Five Lamps records: The Chan master Yangshan Huiji went to study with the Chan master Weishan Lingyou and asked, 'What is the true Buddha's abiding place?' Weishan said:

'By the wonder of thinking non-thought, turn back to reflect on the inexhaustible spirit-flame. When thinking is exhausted one returns to the source, where nature and characteristics forever abide, where phenomena and principle are not two, and the true Buddha is thus, thus.'
The master (Yangshan) awakened instantly at these words.

[Si wu si (thinking non-thought)] Thinking that non-thinking (being aware of that no-thought), that is, 'thinking the unthinkable' and 'thinking where nothing can be thought.' [Ling yan (spirit-flame)] Is one's own nature. In ancient times there was no term for 'energy'; the 'spirit-flame' of the ancients is what in modern language is called 'spiritual energy.'
Q: I still do not understand; please be more concrete.

A: The concrete methods vary from person to person. You may take 'thinking the unthinkable' to mean 'thinking that which cannot be thought.' For example, let your thoughts drift away to a place farther and farther from you, sinking into deep stillness and peace. Or you may also gather the thoughts inward, drawing them further and further in, sinking into deep stillness and peace. Whether drifting outward or gathering inward,
the aim is to enter a realm beyond speech and thought and yet utterly clear and distinct
. 'Thinking the unthinkable' is the diamond king's sword that cuts off deluded thoughts and emotional broodings.
Q: In 'thinking the unthinkable,' who is it that thinks?
A: It is the manas consciousness, which 'constantly and deliberately thinks,' that does the thinking. The Sixth Patriarch said:
'I tell you students of the Way, strive with the will intent
(the manas consciousness)
(From the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch)

[Heng shen si liang (constant deliberate thinking)] Is the nature of the manas consciousness: passing through the three times without interruption, it examines all phenomena and principles and weighs them in thought. [San shi (the three times)] Past, present, and future. Dharmas that have already arisen and ceased are called the 'past'; dharmas that have arisen but not yet ceased are the 'present'; dharmas that have not yet arisen are the 'future.' [Nu li xu yong yi (strive with the intent)] The manas consciousness constantly deliberates and clings to the objects of mind. Discriminating thought and delusion always arise from it, so Chan practice is precisely to use the manas consciousness to investigate, to dam up the stream of delusion and hold it still, and at the very place where it no longer flows, to look upon one's original face.
Q: In Chan practice one must rouse the sense of doubt; what is the sense of doubt?

A: Raising the 'Wu' huatou means: take up the single word 'Wu' and enter the state of 'thinking the unthinkable' (or 'thinking where nothing can be thought'), and this very 'thinking' is the investigation. This state of investigation is called the sense of doubt, also called the mass of doubt. If the sense of doubt is present, maintain it and continue investigating; if it is lost, immediately rouse the huatou and stir up doubt, that is, 'think the unthinkable' (or 'think where nothing can be thought'). Continue thus, striving to keep the sense of doubt unbroken. As the practice deepens, the sense of doubt lasts longer and longer and resists disturbance more and more, until all thoughts suddenly cease and stillness and movement become one.

Raising the word 'Wu' is neither to stare at the thought of the word 'Wu,' nor to question and interrogate the 'Wu,' but to 'think the unthinkable' (or 'think where nothing can be thought'). Since beginningsless eons, beings have made thinking a habit, and constant deliberate thinking is the mark of the manas consciousness. To cut off delusion by stopping thought is extremely difficult, and once one stops thinking one is apt to sink into dullness. Now, using 'thinking the unthinkable' to cut off delusion is the art of exchange: because one is thinking, the mind's power is concentrated and one does not sink into dullness; and because what one thinks is the unthinkable (or one thinks where nothing can be thought), there is no delusion and one departs from speech and thought. This is the wonderful method of Chan practice.

Besides jolting oneself awake into the sense of doubt, raising the word 'Wu' has another important function: it jolts one awake to the fact that 'fundamentally there is not a single thing,' and thereby cuts off the defiled thoughts of the dust. Great Master Hanshan said:

'If you cannot abide in patience and are hindered by affliction, the moment you see it rise, take up the Sixth Patriarch's phrase, 'fundamentally there is not a single thing,' like the diamond king's sword, and all affliction at once melts away like ice, and body and mind are transformed into a pool of cool clarity.'
Q: Here it says the sense of doubt is 'thinking the unthinkable,' but some books say the sense of doubt is roused by chasing and investigating the huatou. Which is right?

A: Green willows are everywhere to tether a horse, and every road leads to Chang'an. Although the aim is to awaken one's mind and see the nature, in concrete practice the methods of the various schools need not be alike; they only seek real results. Thus the benevolent see benevolence, and the wise see wisdom.
Q: What is small doubt? What is great doubt?

A: If the sense of doubt lasts a short time and resists disturbance weakly, it is called small doubt; if it lasts long and resists disturbance strongly, it is called great doubt. The school often says: great doubt, great awakening; small doubt, small awakening; no doubt, no awakening. In practicing, the huatou must first stand firm. To say the huatou stands firm means that within a brief time one can maintain the sense of doubt. Then the huatou must stand long. Further, the huatou must resist disturbance; whatever the circumstances, the moment the huatou is raised it stands firm and stands long, as it is said, 'the huatou once raised, deluded thoughts all vanish.' Going on thus, as time passes and the practice matures, until all thoughts suddenly cease and stillness and movement become one. This is the prelude to awakening the mind and seeing the nature; the ancients likened it to:
'the smoke flying from the drilling of the fire-stick, the sign that precedes the fire.'
In his Autobiographical Chronicle, the elder Master Xuyun records how, during a seven-day Chan retreat at Gaomin Temple, he awakened to his mind and saw the nature, writing:

'The office within the meditation hall does not assign me to rotating duty, so I found the leisure to practice. From then on all thoughts suddenly ceased, the practice settled into the seat, day and night became one, and my movement was as swift as flight
(meaning during the running-incense)

. One evening, as the night incense was released, I opened my eyes and suddenly saw a great light as bright as day, transparent within and without; I saw the incense-lamp master relieving himself beyond the wall, and saw the west-rank master in the latrine
(qing, the toilet)

, and far off, boats moving on the river, with trees of every hue on both banks, all of which I could see plainly; only then did the three wooden clappers sound. The next day I asked the incense-lamp master and the west-rank master, and it was indeed so. I knew this was a state, but did not find it strange. By the eighth 'seven' of the twelfth month
(the eighth of the seven-day periods; this session was twelve consecutive seven-day periods)

, on the third evening, when the incense of the sixth stick was ending and the relieving bell had rung, the one tending the retreat as usual poured hot water and splashed it onto my hand, and the teacup fell to the ground. At the sound of its shattering the root of doubt was cut off at once, and I was glad as never before in my life, as if waking from a dream. ... Therefore I composed this verse: The cup fell and struck the ground, the sound rang clear and distinct, empty space was shattered, and the wild mind was instantly stilled.'
Q: What is the difference between Chan practice and cultivating concentration (samadhi)?

A: Cultivating concentration is to gather the mind so that it does not move, whereas Chan practice is to maintain the sense of doubt throughout, that is, 'thinking the unthinkable' (or 'thinking where nothing can be thought'). The Chan master Boshan Yuanlai said:

'When one sits long one accords with the state of stillness, dimly unknowing, cut off and utterly without relation; even if one gains concentration and gathers the mind so that it does not move, how does this differ from the Lesser Vehicles?'
(From the Chan Admonitions of Master Boshan)
Q: Please explain concretely how to raise the word 'Wu' throughout the twenty-four hours.

A: The Dharma has no fixed Dharma; the wonder of its application lies in the one mind. Each person's circumstances differ, so one must apply it concretely within concrete situations. In principle: follow the path of 'a myriad thoughts returning to one, the one returning to nothing.' As long as one reaches the state of 'all thoughts suddenly resting still, stillness and movement becoming one' (which the school calls 'the practice settling into the seat'), awakening the mind and seeing the nature is only a matter of time. For example, if through the practice in the preceding chapters one can enter directly into the practice of 'the one returning to nothing,' then enter directly; if one cannot yet, then first undertake the practice of 'a myriad thoughts returning to one.' The practice of a myriad thoughts returning to one is, throughout the twenty-four hours, keeping the 'Wu' huatou constantly raised, allowing only the single thought of 'Wu' (or no thought) and nothing else. Because circumstances keep changing through the day, the application of the 'Wu' huatou varies accordingly. For example, when sitting in meditation or before sleep, the word 'Wu' is a command; as soon as the word 'Wu' is raised, one enters the state of 'thinking the unthinkable.' If one is attending to guests and there is no need to speak, then just guard the word 'Wu.' In some situations the word 'Wu' commands us to enter the thought-free state. Because through the practice of 'awareness of thoughts' in the preceding chapter one has already gained the ability to dwell, for a brief time, in the thought-free state, one can raise the word 'Wu' and enter it immediately; when deluded thoughts do not arise, there is no need to raise it again, and if they do arise, raise it at once, practicing especially at the place where the mind stirs in daily life. As said before, raising the word 'Wu' has yet another important function: to jolt one awake to the fact that 'fundamentally there is not a single thing.' Whenever circumstances entangle one, raising the word 'Wu' is the Sixth Patriarch's 'fundamentally there is not a single thing,' and with a single stroke of the sword all the thousand threads are cut, all affliction at once melts like ice, and body and mind are transformed into a pool of cool clarity.

What is said above is only a general indication. One should firmly grasp the path of practice of 'a myriad thoughts returning to one, the one returning to nothing,' responding to circumstances as they arise, and gradually establish, through practice, a method capable of 'resolving the specific problem within the specific situation.' Practicing thus over a long time, when the skill has deepened, whether one is attentive or not, in whatever circumstances, one dwells always in 'thinking the unthinkable.' And once thinking is exhausted and one returns to the source, one sees the true Buddha.
Q: How does one raise the word 'Wu' while working?

A: When working, one should concentrate one's mind entirely on the work; as long as one's whole attention is on the work, that is raising the word 'Wu.' Be careful never to fall into the state of 'working while entertaining delusions.' Once you sink into that, immediately raise the word 'Wu,' cut off the delusion, and return to the state of concentrated work.

If you are doing housework or repetitive labor, you may practice in this way: raise the word 'Wu' and immediately enter the thought-free state. This thought-free state is the sense of doubt. When the sense of doubt is present, there is no need to raise the huatou; when it is absent, raise it at once. First let the sense of doubt stand firm, then let it stand long, then let it resist disturbance. At first one is doing the work of a myriad thoughts returning to one, and then of the one returning to nothing.
The Chan master Wuliangcang of White Cloud in Chuzhou said:

'Throughout the twenty-four hours, walk with the huatou, stand with the huatou, sit with the huatou, lie down with the huatou. The mind is like a bur of the jujube thorn, not to be swallowed up by any self and other, ignorance, the five desires, the three poisons, and so forth. In walking, standing, sitting, and lying, the whole body is one mass of doubt. Doubting this way and that, all day long like a wooden block, when one hears a sound and sees a form, take care, the time will come when it breaks open with a 'po'!'
(From the Guan cejin, 'Encouragement for the Chan Gate')

[The five desires] Form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch. Form means lovely appearances; sound means melodious voices; fragrance means sweet scents; taste means delicious flavors; touch means pleasant sensations of contact. Because these five can give rise to a mind of craving, they are called the five desires. In the Sutra of Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching, the Buddha says:
"You should restrain the five faculties; do not let them run loose and enter the five desires."

[The three poisons] Greed, anger, and delusion. Greed is craving for the five desires; anger is resentment and intolerance; delusion is foolishness and ignorance. Because greed, anger, and delusion can poison both our physical life and our life of wisdom, they are called the "three poisons"; they are also the root of all afflictions.
Question: Can one, in any situation whatsoever, simply raise the word "no" and thereby enter the state of "thinking the unthinkable"?

Answer: If you can do this, so much the better. Ordinarily this is the state of one whose practice has already grown deep. In cultivation there are two gates: effortless accord and remedial counteraction. The gate of effortless accord is like a boatman riding the tide, rising and falling with the raging waves without capsizing. If you cannot manage that, then first enter the gate of remedial counteraction: whatever problem arises, deal with that problem directly, never letting a single thought slip past. At the stage of practice called "ten thousand thoughts returning to one," any method that can gather the mind into oneness is a good method. The more effective your "ten thousand thoughts returning to one" becomes, the more naturally your practice of "thinking the unthinkable" will come into its own.
Question: In practice I have found that using the word "think" as a huatou works very well. The moment I raise this huatou, I enter the state of "thinking the unthinkable." May I do this?

Answer: It is excellent that through practice you have found your own huatou. The ancients likened the huatou to a tile used to knock on a door: its purpose is to open the door so that you may see the person inside. So what kind of tile it is does not matter; what matters is that it opens the door. In the instructions of Patriarch Dahui, all kinds of huatou were used to guide students.
Question: When I practice "thinking the unthinkable" in stillness, I benefit greatly. But when I practice it in the midst of activity, I find it very difficult. What should I do?

Answer: In that case, practice presence in the midst of activity. Raise the single word "no" and you enter presence. The state of presence is none other than the mass of doubt. (For presence in detail, see Chapter Four, "Awareness of the Present Moment.")
Question: Since ancient times there have been so many instructions on the methods of Chan practice that students hardly know which to follow. Please choose among them for us.
Answer: Instructions on seeing the nature through Chan practice first appear in the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch. The Sixth Patriarch instructed Huiming, saying:
"Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, at just such a moment, that
(that is, which)
one is the original face of Venerable Ming?"

At these words Huiming was greatly awakened. "Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, at just such a moment" is the instant before a single thought has arisen. So the method of seeing the nature is this: at the instant before a single thought has arisen, turn the light around and reflect -- what is your original face? For one of the highest faculties, this single phrase is enough; hence Huiming was greatly awakened at these words. But for an ordinary person, to be able to "turn the light around and reflect, at the instant before a single thought has arisen, on what the original face is," one must first be able to abide in a stable state of no-thought, that is, to have the practice of unbroken no-thought reach the stage of single continuity. And for no-thought to become single continuity, one must first have the foundation of "ten thousand thoughts returning to one." Therefore seeing the nature through Chan practice involves three stages of work: first, ten thousand thoughts returning to one; second, the one returning to nothing; third, seeing one's own nature. In order to establish the foundation of "ten thousand thoughts returning to one" quickly, there are various preliminary practices (for example, the preliminary chapters of
Chan of Awareness

). After seeing one's own nature (breaking through the first gate), there is still the work of preserving and nurturing the realization (breaking through the second and third gates). The many instructions on Chan methods found in koans and recorded sayings are nothing other than explanations of how to do the preliminaries, how to bring ten thousand thoughts to one, how to return the one to nothing, how to see one's own nature, what the awakened state of seeing the nature is like, and how to preserve and nurture it after awakening (subduing afflictions, cutting off afflictions, and awakening to the unborn). You may choose among them according to your present situation.
Question: What is the key to the work of Chan practice?

Answer: The key to the work of Chan practice is this: let go of the bag of skin (this body), raise a single thought alone, and work at it finely and continuously, never letting it be interrupted. Old Master Xuyun said:

"This shell of ours, once the breath stops, is a corpse. The only reason we cannot let it go is that we prize it, and so we give rise to ideas of self and other, right and wrong, love and hate, taking and rejecting. If we were certain that this shell is a corpse, did not treasure it, and simply did not take it as "I," what would there be that we could not let go of? Once you can let go, then throughout the twelve periods of the day, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, whether in activity or stillness, at leisure or in busyness, the whole body inside and out is just one mass of doubt. Doubt on, calmly and evenly, without a thread of stray thought mixed in. A single huatou is like a long sword leaning against the sky: when a demon comes, cut the demon; when a Buddha comes, cut the Buddha. Fear no delusive thought. What can disturb you? Who bothers to divide activity from stillness? Who bothers to cling to existence or emptiness? If you fear delusive thoughts, you have added one more delusive thought; if you feel pure, you are no longer pure; if you fear falling into emptiness, you have already fallen into existence; if you want to become a Buddha, you have already entered the demonic path. As it is said: carrying water and hauling firewood are nothing but the wondrous path; hoeing fields and tilling soil are always Chan opportunity. It is not only when you sit cross-legged in meditation all day that you count as working at the Way."
The heart of ox-herding is this: to purify and remove the streaming consciousness that manifests karma within one's own mind.
When a delusive thought arises, that is "the ox wandering off into the grass"; you must then use the huatou to "seize it by the nose and drag it back."

The work of preserving and nurturing the realization after seeing the nature is like herding an ox (the mind is the ox, the huatou is the nose-rope, and the master is the herd boy); hence it is called the practice of ox-herding.

[The nose-rope] For a Chan practitioner investigating a huatou, the huatou is the nose-rope. For one who sees the nature through direct pointing (as in the case below, where Lan'an saw his nature through the guidance of Chan Master Baizhang), watching the mind (watching the present thought) is the nose-rope.
The Notes from the Jade Forest of the Chan Garden records:

Long ago, Lan'an came to visit Chan Master Baizhang. After bowing, he asked, "This student wishes to know the Buddha; which one is it?" Baizhang said, "It is much like riding an ox while searching for the ox
(your own nature is the Buddha, so what is the point of wishing to know the Buddha).
" He asked, "After recognizing it, what then
(after recognizing the Buddha, that is, after seeing the nature, what then)
?" Baizhang said, "It is like a person riding the ox home
(cultivating in accord with the nature, so that the self-nature returns to its source)
." He asked, "I do not yet understand how one should preserve and nurture it from beginning to end
(not knowing how, on the road home, one should preserve and nurture it from first to last)
?" Baizhang said, "Like an ox-herder who holds a staff and watches it, not letting it trample the seedlings
(cutting off habitual tendencies thought by thought, as one meets circumstances and conditions)

[Preserving and nurturing] Preserving and according with conditions are the two stages of purifying away habitual tendencies after seeing the nature. "Preserving" means doing one's utmost to care for the sacred embryo so that it suffers no harm from greed, anger, or delusion, thereby accomplishing the first two of the four forbearances (the forbearance of subjugation and the forbearance of gentle compliance). "According with conditions" means that once the sacred embryo has grown to adulthood, it operates naturally in accord with circumstances, being tempered further amid favorable and unfavorable conditions, thereby accomplishing the last two of the four forbearances (the forbearance of the unborn and the forbearance of quiescent extinction). [The four forbearances] The forbearance of subjugation, the forbearance of gentle compliance, the forbearance of the unborn, and the forbearance of quiescent extinction. The forbearance of subjugation: the beginner who wishes to forbear favorable and unfavorable conditions (without giving rise to greed, anger, or delusion) must first tame and subdue the mind. The forbearance of gentle compliance: having tamed the mind for a long time, one meets circumstances and conditions and can forbear naturally without forced restraint (without giving rise to greed, anger, or delusion); at that point the mind is gentle, harmonious, and compliant. The forbearance of the unborn: one who has reached the stage of the sages understands that all dharmas are fundamentally unborn, that sentient and insentient alike arise from conditions and have no nature of their own, and are empty just as they are; therefore, within the natureless dharma, the forbearing mind does not move, and one personally realizes the unborn. The forbearance of quiescent extinction: the sage at the fruition stage thoroughly realizes the quiescent state of nirvana, and both the aspects of motion and stillness accord with suchness. [Suchness] The state of self-nature in which no inverted discrimination arises. Because it is the true suchness (the true reality of all dharmas) realized by the wisdom of suchness, it is called "suchness."
Old Master Yuanyin's
A Brief Discussion of Understanding the Mind and Seeing the Nature
says:
Now that one has awakened to the Way
(seen one's own nature)

, although one has already clearly awakened to the fact that one's own empty, quiescent spiritual awareness is the true Buddha, yet because the habitual defilements of many lives run deep, they cannot be suddenly erased all at once; when things happen the mind still moves, and when circumstances appear it is still hard to be free of thought. Yet when the mind moves and thoughts arise, one is not like the blind, who do not know that the objects of sense are fundamentally empty and so cling and grasp, wandering on and forgetting to return. Rather, when the preceding thought moves, the following thought is immediately aware and instantly sweeps it away. It is only that, compared with one whose mind never moves at all, there remain traces of arising and ceasing and the power is somewhat weaker. But if one can preserve and nurture finely and continuously, aware and illumining at every moment, then as days pass and the work deepens, one will naturally become a single continuity. The ox-herding practice of the patriarchs of every generation is the model for this work after awakening.""Therefore one must cultivate thought after thought, be aware and illumine mind after mind: after the great awakening, in regard to evil, cut off evil, yet cut off while cutting off nothing
(without clinging to marks)

, and in regard to good, cultivate good, yet cultivate while cultivating nothing; then one enters the hall and the inner chamber, returns home, and sits securely at ease -- such a one is called "the idle wayfarer of no more learning and no doing.""

blocks.text: Chan Master Puming's Verses on the Ten Ox-Herding Pictures

inline.s: In these pictures the ox changes from black to white, marking the mind's passage from defilement and agitation into purity and quiescence.

(1) Not Yet Herded: Fierce are its horns, it bellows wild and free; / it runs the streams and hills and strays from me. / A black cloud hangs across the valley's mouth; / who knows each step tramples the tender sprout?

This describes the state of the mind-ox before it has been herded: "Fierce are its horns, it bellows wild and free" depicts the wildness of the mind-ox; "it runs the streams and hills and strays from me" means that the mind-ox dashes east and west, getting farther and farther from home; "A black cloud hangs across the valley's mouth" is the hidden danger -- fall into it and you are smashed to pieces; "who knows each step tramples the tender sprout" means that the mind-ox is breaking the rules at every moment and in every place.

(2) First Taming: I have a coarse rope threaded through its nose; / each time it bolts, the whip falls hard and close. / Its stubborn nature long has scorned the rein; / the mountain boy must tug with all his strength again.

This describes the first taming of the mind-ox: "I have a coarse rope threaded through its nose" means threading the ox-nose rope (the huatou) through the mind-ox's nose; "each time it bolts, the whip falls hard and close" means that whenever the mind gives rise to a delusive thought, one redoubles the effort of practice; "Its stubborn nature long has scorned the rein; the mountain boy must tug with all his strength again" means that at this point the mind-ox will not submit, so not a single thought may relax the huatou -- the nose-rope (the huatou) must hold the mind-ox back and not let it sink into delusive thought.

(3) Under Control: By slow degrees it yields and checks its flight; / through streams and clouds it follows, pace by pace. / My hand still holds the rope, nor slackens quite; / the herd boy forgets his toil in that quiet place.

This describes the mind-ox under control: "By slow degrees it yields and checks its flight" means that after taming, the mind-ox no longer races about and delusive thoughts grow fewer and fewer; "through streams and clouds it follows, pace by pace" means that the moment the huatou is raised, delusive thoughts vanish entirely; "My hand still holds the rope, nor slackens quite" means that one still dares not relax in the slightest; "the herd boy forgets his toil in that quiet place" means that because the mind-ox has finally been subdued, the herd boy now delights in it and forgets his fatigue.

(4) Turning Its Head: Long days of practice turn its head at last; / its frantic heart grows patient, mild, and slow. / The mountain boy will not yet trust it fully; / he keeps the rope and will not let it go.

This describes how the mind-ox no longer resists (turning its head, that is, turning its mind around): "Long days of practice turn its head at last; its frantic heart grows patient, mild, and slow" means that the mind-ox no longer resists; "The mountain boy will not yet trust it fully" means that the herd boy still dares not trust the mind-ox completely; "he keeps the rope and will not let it go" means that the huatou (the rope) still may not be put down.

(5) Tamed and Subdued: Beneath green willows by the old stream's side / it comes and goes, at ease and free from fear. / At dusk, blue clouds and fragrant meadows wide -- / the herd boy walks on home, no rope to steer.
This describes the mind-ox already obedient: the huatou need no longer be raised (the nose-rope may be coiled away), and one enters the state of no-thought.
(6) Unobstructed: In open ground it sleeps, at ease and free; / no whip, no goad, forever unconfined. / The mountain boy sits calm beneath the tree; / a song of peace leaves ample joy behind.

This describes the mind-ox already unobstructed: it no longer breaks the rules or gets in the way (the state of no-thought is already very stable, with no delusive thoughts), and the herd boy is calm and at ease.

(7) According with Conditions: Amid spring waves and willows, evening glow, / faint mist and tender grass of velvet green, / it eats when hungry, drinks when thirsty, letting hours go; / the mountain boy sleeps deep on stone, serene.

This describes the mind-ox having entered the state of according with conditions: it now "follows what its heart desires without overstepping the rule," so the herd boy simply lets go and pays it no more heed.

(8) Mutual Forgetting: The white ox ever dwells in white clouds high; / the man is mindless, and the ox is so. / The moon shines through, and all the clouds turn white; / white clouds and moon drift east or west -- let go.
This describes the mutual forgetting of herd boy and mind-ox: the herd boy has completely forgotten the mind-ox, letting the mind be free.

(9) Alone Illumining: The ox is gone; the herd boy idles still; / one lonely cloud hangs in the blue peaks' height. / He claps and sings beneath the moon at will; / yet one more gate remains before the light.

This describes the condition in which the illuminating essence stands alone: the mind-ox is gone, but the herd boy remains. Because the mind-ox has been dissolved, the herd boy naturally has nothing to do and is free and at ease, "clapping his hands and singing beneath the bright moon"; yet this is not yet ultimate, for the herd boy too must be dissolved. Hence the verse says, "Returning home, one gate remains" -- that is, before he can reach home there is still the gate of "dissolving the herd boy."

(10) Both Dissolved: No man, no ox, no trace where they have gone; / the moon's cold light -- ten thousand forms are bare. / If you would ask the true meaning of this song, / wild flowers and fragrant grasses cluster there.
This describes the mutual dissolution of herd boy and mind-ox, the ultimate and perfect state.

blocks.text: Master Kuo'an's Verses on the Ten Ox-Herding Pictures, with Preface

inline.s: (1) Searching for the Ox. It was never lost, so why search for it? Because one turns away from awakening, one grows estranged; because one faces the dusts, one loses it. The home mountain recedes, and the forked road is suddenly missed
(missed, that is, erred and gone astray)
. Gain and loss blaze up, and right and wrong bristle like spears.

The verse says: In haste I part the grass and search around; / wide waters, distant hills, the deeper way. / My strength is spent -- where can it yet be found? / Only the maple and late cicadas sing at close of day.

(2) Seeing the Traces. One understands the meaning according to the sutras, and reading the traces knows the track. One realizes that many vessels are one gold, and comprehends all things as oneself. Right and wrong are not yet distinguished; true and false -- how are they told apart? Not yet having entered this gate, one provisionally sees the traces.
[Realizing that many vessels are one gold] Understanding that although the many golden vessels differ in shape, they are in fact all made of gold.
The verse says: By stream and under tree the traces lie; / among the scattered grasses -- do you see? / Even in the deepest mountains, mountain-high, / how could that vast-sky nostril hide from me?

[Among the scattered grasses -- do you see?] One sees only the fragrant grasses scattered and intermingled. [Scattered] Loose; intermingled. [Do you see?] A filler phrase with no meaning. In the Tang poet Zhongli Quan's poem "To Lu Dongbin": "Though one expounds a thousand subtle, wondrous truths, your heart may still not believe -- do you see?"

(3) Seeing the Ox. One enters by way of sound, and at every point of seeing meets the source. At the six sense-gates every move is without error; in all activity and function it stands revealed at every turn. Saltness in water, blue dye in color. The instant one blinks, it is no other thing.

[Saltness in water, blue dye in color] When salt dissolves in water, one can taste its saltiness but cannot see its form; when white cloth is dyed, one sees only the color but cannot see the form of the dye. [Blue dye] Pigment; dyestuff.

The verse says: Upon the branch the oriole sings, note on note; / the sun is warm, the breeze is kind, the willows green. / For this there is no place of turning, no retreat; / those branching, forest-thick horns can scarce be seen.
(4) Getting the Ox. Long hidden in the outskirts, today I meet with it
(that is, with him)

. Because it is so swift, the fine terrain is hard to pursue; it clings to the fragrant thickets without cease. Its stubborn mind is still bold, its wild nature still remains. If one would have it pure and gentle, one must apply the whip.

The verse says: With all my powers of mind I have caught it at last; / its heart is strong, its body stout -- not soon subdued. / Sometimes it climbs the high plateaus and travels fast, / then plunges into mist and haze, in deep retreat renewed.

(5) Herding and Guarding. The former thought has just arisen, and the latter thought follows after. Because of awakening it becomes true; because of delusion it becomes false. It does not come into being from circumstances, but arises only from one's own mind. Hold the nose-rope firmly; allow no deliberation.
The verse says: The whip and rope I never let them leave my side, / lest it step out and stir the dust of earth. / Together we have herded it to gentleness; / the unseen fetter follows me henceforth.
[Follows the person] The ox has been herded into tameness and follows one step by step.

(6) Riding Home. The weapons of war are laid down; gain and loss are no more. I sing the village songs of the woodcutter and pipe the rustic tunes of children. Lying across the ox's back, my eyes on the clouds of heaven. Call and it will not come back; no net can
(that is, enclose)
hold it.

The verse says: Astride the ox, by winding ways, I turn for home; / the nomad flute note after note sends off the day. / One clap, one song, a meaning words can never say -- / for one who knows the tune, the lips need never move.

(7) The Person Remains. In the Dharma there are no two dharmas; the ox itself is the essential teaching. It is like the different names of the snare and the rabbit, or the distinction between the fish-trap and the fish. It is as gold coming forth from ore, as the moon emerging from cloud. One cold shaft of light, beyond the kalpa of Wondrous Sound.

[The snare and the fish-trap] The snare is a tool for catching rabbits; the fish-trap is a tool for catching fish. Zhuangzi, "External Things," says: "The fish-trap exists for the sake of the fish; once you have the fish, you forget the trap. The snare exists for the sake of the rabbit; once you have the rabbit, you forget the snare. Words exist for the sake of meaning; once you have the meaning, you forget the words." [Having the fish and forgetting the trap] A metaphor for having reached the goal and therefore forgetting the means. [Wondrous Sound] Wondrous Sound King Buddha, the Buddha at the beginning of the kalpa. [Beyond the kalpa of Wondrous Sound] Before the beginning of the kalpa.

The verse says: Astride the ox, at last I reach my native hill; / the ox is void, and now the man is still. / The sun is three poles high, and yet I dream; / the whip and rope lie idle by the thatched hall's beam.

(8) Both Forgotten. Ordinary feelings fall away, and holy meaning is emptied out. Where there is a Buddha, one need not linger; where there is no Buddha, one must hurry past. Attached to neither extreme, one is hard even for a thousand eyes to spy. A hundred birds bearing flowers -- a matter for shame.

[A hundred birds bearing flowers] A hundred birds came bearing flowers in offering. Before Chan Master Niutou Farong had met Daoxin, the Fourth Patriarch of Chan, he had already attained the state in which a hundred birds bore flowers to present to him. The Fourth Patriarch, observing the auspices from afar, knew that there was an extraordinary person on that mountain and went in person to seek him out. After meeting him, he pointed out the way to him, and thereafter the birds no longer bore flowers. [Moluo (mo luo)] A Sanskrit word, translated into Chinese as "shame." [A hundred birds bearing flowers -- a matter for shame] A matter for shame and regret. This says that before Farong met the Fourth Patriarch, he vainly supposed that "a hundred birds bearing flowers" was the ultimate state. (See in detail
The Fourth Patriarch's Instruction to Farong

) The Continued Essential Sayings of the Ancient Venerable Masters says: "It was asked, 'When Niutou had not yet seen the Fourth Patriarch, why did a hundred birds come bearing flowers?' The master said, 'Wealth and honor are what people desire.' It was asked, 'After he saw him, why did they no longer bear flowers?' The master said, 'Poverty and lowliness.'" Yang Wuwei said: "The purple vapor spreads and pierces the white clouds; because he met the master craftsman, he was shown the ford. The hundred birds that bore flowers pine away for nothing, for they no longer see the old master in his hut."
The verse says: Whip, rope, and man and ox -- all empty too; / the boundless azure sky no words can say. / Upon the red furnace's flame, how
(how)
can snow find room? Only thus is one joined to the true way.

(9) Returning to the Source. Fundamentally pure, it receives not a speck of dust. One watches the flourishing and withering of that which has marks, and abides in the emptiness and quiescence of the unconditioned. It is not the same as illusion; how could it need cultivation and polishing? Water is green, mountains are blue -- sitting, one watches success and failure.
The verse says: Returning to the root and source has cost me toil; how
(how)
much better it is to be, right here, as though blind and deaf. In the hut, the things before the hut are not seen; the water spreads vast of itself, the flowers are red of themselves.

(10) Entering the Marketplace. The brushwood gate is shut alone; a thousand sages do not know. One buries one's own radiance and turns one's back on the path of the ancient worthies. Carrying a gourd, one enters the market; leaning on a staff, one returns home. In wine shops and fish stalls, one transforms beings and brings them to Buddhahood.
[Chan (marketplace)] An ancient variant of the character for "marketplace," meaning a market.

The verse says: Bare-chested, barefoot, to the market I make my way; / smeared with dirt and ash, my cheeks all wreathed in smiles. / No immortal's secret formula have I to say -- / I only make the withered tree burst forth in flower.
[Xian (barefoot)] Going barefoot.
Patriarch Dahui says:
Since you have taken up this Way
(Chan practice)
, throughout the twelve periods of the day, wherever you meet things and respond to conditions, you must not let evil thoughts
(for
a cultivator
of the Way, delusive thoughts are evil thoughts, because they cut off the life of the dharma-body and wisdom)
continue in succession. If your attention slips and a single evil thought arises, you must at once summon up your energy
(that is, immediately
rouse your spirit
, and pull it back around
turn from delusive thought back to right mindfulness
. If you always
(always)
let it go its own way and continue without interruption, this not only obstructs the Way but marks you as a person without wisdom. Long ago Weishan asked Lan'an
(Chan Master Da'an)
: 'Throughout the twelve periods of the day, what is your task?
(what are you doing in the twenty-four hours?)
Lan'an said, 'Herding an ox.' Weishan said, 'How do you herd it?
(how do you herd it?)
Lan'an said, 'Whenever it goes off into the grass
(when a delusive thought arises)
, I seize it by the nose and drag it back.
(as soon as the ox leaves the true path, one sharply pulls the nose-rope and drags it back.)
Weishan said, 'You
(you)
truly herd the ox!
(you are truly herding the mind-ox!)
When a student of the Way restrains evil thoughts
stops
delusive thoughts)
, he should be like Lan'an herding his ox; then in time he will naturally become thoroughly proficient
(no delusive thought arises)
(from the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dahui Pujue)

[Lan'an] Chan Master Da'an of Changqing in Fuzhou, whose sobriquet was Lan'an (Lazy An), was a son of the Chen family of that prefecture. He received his training on Mount Huangbo and studied the Vinaya. He once thought to himself, "Though I have worked hard, I have never heard the principle of the profound ultimate." So he traveled alone with his staff. On his way to Hongjing he passed through Shangyuan, where he met an old man who told him, "If you go to Nanchang, you will gain something." The master then went to Baizhang and, after bowing, asked, "This student wishes to know the Buddha; which one is it?" Baizhang said, "It is much like riding an ox while searching for the ox." He asked, "After recognizing it, what then?" Baizhang said, "It is like a person riding the ox home." He asked, "I do not yet understand how one should preserve and nurture it from beginning to end." Baizhang said, "Like an ox-herder who holds a staff and watches it, not letting it trample the seedlings
(that is, without delusive thinking)

." From then on the master understood the purport and no longer sought elsewhere. His fellow student Chan Master You founded a dwelling on Mount Wei, and the master plowed in person to support the community. When You entered nirvana, the assembly asked him to succeed as abbot. In the hall he said: "All of you come to An
(you all come to rely on me)
, and seek for what? If you wish to become a Buddha, you are yourself a Buddha. To carry the Buddha about and run to other houses is like a thirsty deer chasing
(chasing)

the mirage -- when will you ever accord with it! If you wish to become a Buddha, simply be free of all that is inverted, of grasping, of delusive thought, of evil perceptions, of defilement and purity; the mind of an ordinary being is itself the Buddha of initial awakening, so where else would you go looking for one! That is why I, An, have stayed on Mount Wei these thirty years, eating Mount Wei's rice and shitting Mount Wei's dung, without studying Mount Wei's Chan. I only watch one water buffalo. If it strays from the path into the grass, I grab its nostrils and pull it back; as soon as it tramples the seedlings, I whip it into submission. After a long time, poor thing, it came to accept my words (it was ashamed to receive everyone's praise), and now it has turned into a white ox in the open ground, always before my eyes, clear and bright all day long, and it cannot be driven away (all day long, clear and bright before my eyes, impossible to drive off)." (From the Notes from the Jade Forest of the Chan Garden.) [Mirage] A vapor produced under the blazing sun, which from afar looks like water; the thirsty long to drink it but can never obtain it -- a metaphor for illusion. One of the ten similes of the Mahayana. [The white ox in the open ground] "Open ground" is the empty space outside the gate, a metaphor for a place of peace and safety; "white ox" means a pure ox. The Lotus Sutra

Chapter on Parables, in which the white ox is used as a simile for the One Vehicle teaching, thereby pointing to a pure state unstained by the slightest affliction as "the white ox in the open ground."
He also says:

"While the mass of doubt is not yet broken, simply look into a huatou by which an ancient entered the Way; take the mind that day after day does nothing but delusive thinking and bring it onto the huatou, and then none of that will work anymore. A monk asked Zhaozhou, 'Does a dog have the Buddha-nature or not?' Zhaozhou said, 'No.' This single word is the knife that cuts off the road of birth and death. When a delusive thought arises, simply raise the word 'no'; raise it again and again, and suddenly the news is cut off -- that is where you sit securely at home. Beyond this there is nothing extraordinary; that step you called hard to take, you will find you have suddenly passed it without knowing."
[Mo
mo
] Sudden, unexpected.
The Gateless Gate says:

"In Chan practice one must pass through the patriarchs' gate; for wondrous awakening, the path of the mind must be exhausted and cut off. If you do not pass the patriarchs' gate and do not cut off the mind's path, you are nothing but a spirit clinging to grass and trees. Tell me, what is the patriarchs' gate? It is just this
(this)

one word 'no' -- it is a gate of our school. Hence it is called 'the Gateless Gate of Chan.' One who passes through it not only sees Zhaozhou face to face, but can walk hand in hand with the patriarchs of every generation, brow to brow with them
(joined as one body)
, seeing with the same eye, hearing with the same ear -- is that not cause for joy
(rejoicing and delight)

? Is there anyone who wants to pass this gate? Take the three hundred and sixty bones and joints, the eighty-four thousand pores, and raise a mass of doubt through your whole body; investigate the word 'no' day and night, keeping it alive. Do not take it as nothingness, do not take it as existence or nonexistence. It is like swallowing a red-hot iron ball that you cannot spit out, sweeping away all your former evil knowing and evil awareness. When in time it becomes pure and ripe, inner and outer will naturally become one continuous whole, like a mute person's dream that only he himself can know. Suddenly it bursts open, shaking heaven and earth, like seizing General Guan's great blade in your hand -- meeting a Buddha, kill the Buddha; meeting a patriarch, kill the patriarch; at the shore of birth and death you attain great freedom, and play in samadhi among the six realms and the four kinds of birth. And how should you keep it alive
(so then, how should one keep it alive?)
? With all the strength of your life raise the word 'no'; if you do not interrupt it, it is like the Dharma candle
(a candle)
-- touch it once and it lights."

[The Gateless Gate] The book The Gateless Gate was compiled by the Song-dynasty Chan monk Wumen Huikai: because students came to him for instruction, he took the koans of the ancients as tiles for knocking at the door and guided learners according to their capacities, jotting them down as they came and unwittingly making a collection. The book cites forty-eight famous koans from antiquity, adding verses and commentaries. Its form is first to cite the case, then to give a commentary, and finally to append his own verse. [The patriarchs' gate] The gate that a patriarch must pass through. Without passing this gate one cannot become a patriarch. The patriarchs' gate is the state of sudden awakening, and the crux of this gate lies in the single word 'no'; only by penetrating this gate can one cut off the mind's path, attain wondrous awakening, and walk hand in hand with the patriarchs of every generation. [Keeping it alive] To stay alert and roused, maintaining right mindfulness. Master Lianchi said, "I hope you will let go of the ten thousand conditions, and in the twelve periods (twenty-four hours) keep it alive in every thought -- this is my greatest wish." (From the Yunqi Collected Works.) The Complete Works of Master Zhu
"Preserving and Nourishing" says: "One need only keep it alive constantly; accumulating little by little, in time it will naturally continue without break and become a single whole."

[Dharma candle] What we today call a candle. "Candle" means a fire that gives light. In the Han dynasty Liu An was the first to make candles to replace oil lamps; the King of Huainan established them as a standard model and promoted them widely, and so they were called "dharma candles."
Before it is thoroughly penetrated, it is like a rat gnawing at a coffin -- there is no shifting it.
In the Continued Record of the Lamp, Chan Master Mengshan Deyi recounts in his own words the course of his Chan practice and awakening:
I
(the master's self-reference)
, at the age of twenty, knew that there was this matter
(understanding the mind and seeing the nature)

. By the age of thirty-two I had sought instruction from seventeen or eighteen elders, asking them about doing the work, and none of them had anything definite. Later I studied under Elder Wanshan, who taught me to look into the word 'no.' Throughout the twelve periods of the day one must stay awake and alert, like a cat catching a mouse or a hen brooding on eggs, never letting it be interrupted. Before it is thoroughly penetrated, it is like a rat gnawing at a coffin
(only by gnawing through can it survive)
, and there is no shifting it. If you go on like this, there will surely come a time of discovery
(when the mind-flower suddenly blooms)
. So day and night I diligently
(untiringly)
investigated it. After eighteen days, while drinking tea
(as I was drinking tea)
, I suddenly understood "the World-Honored One holds up a flower, and Kashyapa smiles," and was overjoyed.
("Suddenly understood" -- this is understanding-awakening, not realization.)

I sought confirmation from three or four elders, and none of them said a word. One taught me simply to seal it with the single seal of the ocean-seal samadhi and pay no heed to anything else. I believed this teaching.

[Xingxing] clear and lucid in awareness. For a cultivator, to fall into deluded thinking or into torpor is to be lacking a lucid mind, because one is not the master of oneself. [Haiyin samadhi] when the delusions are exhausted and the mind grows clear, the myriad phenomena appear together, like the surface of a calm and crystal sea, where no form goes unreflected. The Shurangama Sutra says:
“As I press my finger, the ocean-seal gives forth light; the moment you raise a thought, the dust-labor arises first.”
After two years had passed
(two years having gone by)
, in the fifth year of the reign of Jingding
(the fifth year of Jingding of the Southern Song Dynasty (
, in the sixth month, in Chongqing Prefecture of Sichuan, he fell ill with dysentery
(contracted dysentery)
, passing stools a hundred times by day and by night
(diarrhea a hundred times day and night)
. His condition grew critical, and he was on the verge of death, his practice wholly of no avail
(the practice was entirely powerless)

. The hai-yin samadhi could also not be used; what he had understood before likewise could not be used. He had a mouth but could not speak, a body but could not move; there was nothing but death. The karmic bonds and realms appeared before him at once
(he personally experienced that intellectual understanding cannot overcome birth and death)

, and filled with terror and confusion, all the many sufferings pressed down upon him. So he forced himself to take charge, and entrusted the affairs of his final moments. He raised his meditation cushion high, laid a stick of incense, and slowly rose to sit in stillness, silently praying to the Three Jewels and the dragons and devas, repenting the many unwholesome deeds of his past: if the limit of his life should be reached, may he rely upon the power of prajna and be reborn in right mindfulness, and leave the home life early; if he should recover from this illness, then he would abandon the lay life to become a monk, and quickly attain enlightenment and understanding, to guide many later students.

Having made this vow, he took up the word ‘Wu’ and turned the light back to look within. Before long, his organs moved three or four times, and he simply paid no heed. After a long while, his eyelids did not move. Again after a long while, he no longer felt his body, only the hua-tou continuing without cease. It was evening before he rose, and his illness had receded by half. He sat again until the fourth watch of the third quarter of the night, and all his illnesses receded entirely, his body and mind serene and light.
In the eighth month he traveled to Jiangling and shaved his head
(shaved his head to become a monk)
; after a year he shouldered his bundle and departed
(left the monastery)

on pilgrimage. On the way, while cooking rice, he realized that the practice must be done in a single breath, without break or interruption. When he arrived at the hall of Huanglong, the first time the sleep-demon came, he sat up, roused his spirit, and lightly repelled it. The second time he likewise repelled it. When the third time the sleep-demon came heavily, he went down, bowed and paid respects to pass the time, then took up his cushion again. With the pattern thus set, he took this very moment to
(pack up)

deal with the sleep-demon. At first he slept with a short pillow, then with his arm, and then he no longer laid his body down. After two or three nights, weary day and night, his feet feeling buoyant and unsteady, suddenly before his eyes it was as if the dark clouds opened, and his body was as clear and refreshed as if he had just bathed in new water. The mass of doubt in his heart grew ever greater, yet without applied effort it flowed on ceaselessly. All sounds and forms, the five desires and the eight winds, could not enter. Pure and clean, like a silver basin filled with snow, like the austere clarity of autumn air.

[Five desires] form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch. Form refers to beautiful appearances; sound to melodious tones; fragrance to sweet scents; taste to delicious flavors; touch to agreeable contact. Because these five can give rise to a mind of greed in beings, they are called the five desires. [Eight winds] gain, loss, slander, praise, fame, derision, suffering, and joy.
Yet he reflected that though the practice was good, there was no one to resolve and choose
(no good-knowing one to cut off his doubts and sort out the principles)
. He shouldered his bundle
(thereupon left the monastery to seek instruction)

and entered Zhejiang; the toil of the road caused his practice to regress. When he arrived at the hall of the solitary toad monk of Chengtian, he made a vow: until enlightenment was attained, he would not leave the monastery
(he would never leave this monastery)
. After a month or so, his practice was restored
(the practice recovered)
. At that time his whole body broke out in sores, yet he paid no heed, risking his life in pursuing
(investigating)
, and the practice naturally gained strength, so that he could also practice amid the toil of illness.
Because he went out to attend a meal, and walked along holding up the hua-tou, without realizing it he passed the house of the meal, and so he also did the practice amid activity.
At this point
it was like moonlight seen through water
at this time, the mass of doubt was like the reflection of the moon seen through water
: upon a rapid torrent, amid the turbulent waves, it could not be scattered, could not be washed away, alive and lively.
On the sixth day of the third month, while sitting he was just raising the word ‘Wu’. The head monk entered the hall to light incense, and made a sound striking the incense box. Suddenly
with a great crack he recognized himself
(recognized his original face; this is realization)
, and defeated Zhaozhou
(pierced through Zhaozhou’s ‘Wu’ gong-an)
. Thereupon he composed a verse saying: The path for one without good fortune is at an end
(ill fortune)
; treading over the waves, he realized the waves are water
(he realized that waves are nothing but water)
; the transcendently admirable old Zhaozhou
(the outstanding old monk Zhaozhou)
, his face is only thus
(his original face is no different from what I have realized)
[Bobo
bō bō
] lively, full of vitality.
In the autumn, at Lin’an he met the great elders Xueyan, Tuigeng, Shikeng, and Xuzhou, and Xuzhou urged him to go to Wanshan. The mountain
(when he reached Wanshan, Master Chan of Yugui on Wanshan)

asked: ‘The bright light, calm and shining, fills the Ganges sands—is this not the saying of Scholar Zhang Zhuo?’ The moment I opened my mouth, the mountain shouted me out. From then on, whether walking, sitting, eating, or drinking, he had no sense of anything. After six months, in the following spring, as he went out of the city and returned, climbing the stone steps, suddenly the obstruction of doubt in his chest melted like ice; he did not know there was a body walking along the road. Then he saw the mountain, and the mountain again asked the former words, and he overturned the meditation bench. Thereupon the several most confusing gong-an from before, he understood each and every one.
[The bright light, calm and shining, fills the Ganges sands—is this not the saying of Scholar Zhang Zhuo?]
This was the master Chan of Yugui on Wanshan making him investigate the gatha of Zhang Zhuo, causing him to wipe out both being and nonbeing.
The Records of the Five Lamps of the Transmission of the Lamp records:
Because the Chan-master of the moon of Zen pointed him to go study under Shishuang
(Scholar Zhang Zhuo, at the guidance of the Chan-master of the moon of Zen, went to call upon Master Shishuang)
. Shishuang asked: ‘What is the scholar’s surname?’ He said: ‘My surname is Zhang, my given name Zhuo.’ Shishuang said: ‘To seek the clever is already unattainable; whence does the clumsy come?’

(To seek skill is already impossible—where then is there clumsiness? This is Master Shishuang speaking of the real nature of all dharmas on the basis of Zhang Zhuo’s name, guiding him into the nondual dharma-mind.)
The scholar
(Zhang Zhuo)
suddenly had an awakening
(a sudden, great enlightenment)
. Thereupon he presented a gatha saying:

The bright light, calm and shining, fills the Ganges’ sands so wide;
Sage and common, every living soul, with me in one house abide.

When not a single thought arises, the whole is shown in sight;
