The six senses once astir, its radiance is veiled from light.

To cut off all afflictions but renews the sickness sore;
To incline toward true suchness is still a wrong shore.

Following worldly conditions, without a single cling;
Rebirth and nirvana are but empty flowers on the wing.
This gatha was written by Zhang Zhuo after his great awakening, describing his own state, and presented to Master Shishuang, asking him to verify it. Now I will explain this gatha as follows:
[The bright light, calm and shining, fills the Ganges sands]
speaks of the vision of thoroughly seeing one’s own nature at the moment of enlightenment: the nature’s light, calm and shining, illumines countless great worlds like the sands of the Ganges.
[Sage and common, every living soul, with me in one house abide]

The self-nature of the ordinary person and the sage is the same as that one of mine (the self-nature). Containing spirit refers to beings with sentience, meaning sentient beings, though in this line it refers to the self-nature. This line says that ordinary persons and sages have a self-nature identical to mine; one whose self-nature is deluded is the ordinary person, and one whose self-nature is awakened is the sage.
[When not a single thought arises, the whole is shown in sight]
When not a single thought arises (coarse thoughts, subtle thoughts, and the most subtle thoughts all come to rest), then the nature is thoroughly revealed (the whole appears).
[The six senses once astir, its radiance is veiled from light]
The moment the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) stir, the nature’s original light is covered by affliction, manifesting in the state of habitual propensities.
[To cut off all afflictions but renews the sickness sore]

The self-nature is spiritually luminous, calm, and quiescent, endowed with all virtues, perfect and complete in itself. To stir the mind up to cut off afflictions is instead to add confusion. The Cultivating Mind Discourse says:

“Not knowing that good and evil nature is empty, to sit firmly and still, suppressing body and mind like stone crushing grass, and take this to be cultivation of mind—this is a great confusion! Therefore it is said: ‘The sravaka, thought after thought, cuts off delusion
(the delusions of views and thought)

, and the mind that can cut off is a thief.’ But look closely: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and false speech arise from nature; arising is no-arising, and where they arise they are already quiescent—why must they be cut off? Therefore it is said: ‘Do not fear the arising of thoughts, only fear that awareness is slow.’ And again: ‘When a thought arises, be aware of it; being aware, it is gone.’ Thus in the case of the awakened one, though guest-dust afflictions may remain, they all become the finest cream. If you but illuminate that delusion is without a root, the triple world of flowers in space is like wind rolling up smoke, and the illusory six dusts are like hot water melting ice.”

But note that after enlightenment there are two gates of practice: the gate of free flowing and the gate of remedial counteracting. “To cut off all afflictions but renews the sickness sore” and the next line, “to incline toward true suchness is still a wrong shore,” speak of the gate of free flowing; if one has attained enlightenment but lacks a solid foundation, with afflictions strong and habitual propensities deep, unable to do what is meant by “if you but illuminate that delusion is without a root, the triple world of flowers in space is like wind rolling up smoke, and the illusory six dusts are like hot water melting ice,” then one should first enter the gate of remedial counteracting, and by no means cling falsely to “cutting off afflictions but renews the sickness” and so act “free and at ease.”

[The delusions of views and thought] The delusion of views and the delusion of thought. The delusion of views is the confused errors of ordinary beings in their views, such as the five wrong views: the view of self, the view of extremes, the perverted view, the view of grasping at views, and the view of grasping at prohibitions and precepts. The delusion of thought is the confused errors of ordinary beings in their thinking, such as the afflictions of greed, anger, ignorance, pride, and doubt. These two delusions are the root of sentient beings’ wandering through the cycle of birth and death; cutting them off, one can put an end to birth and death and escape the cycle.
[The finest cream] A dairy product refined many times over, first in flavor and first among medicines. The Great Nirvana Sutra says:
“The finest cream is called the first supreme flavor of the world.”
And again it says:
“Among all medicines the finest cream is first, and it well cures the feverish, troubled minds of sentient beings.”
[To incline toward true suchness is still a wrong shore]

To stir the mind to incline toward suchness (the nature) is also a mistake, because for the nature to manifest its true state, not only coarse and subtle thoughts must come to rest, but even the most subtle thoughts must come to rest—how could one stir the mind to return to the origin (to incline toward it)?
[Following worldly conditions, without a single cling]

Now that one has awakened to the supreme truth of the first meaning, one follows worldly conditions and lives out one’s days transforming beings without any obstruction; when conditions come, one gives; when conditions go, one is still.
[The truth of the first meaning] the supreme, perfect, and final truth, that is, the real nature of all dharmas. The Buddha says:

“All dharmas are false and illusory; where they cease to be is called true, is called real form, is called the dharma-realm, is called final wisdom, is called the truth of the first meaning, is called the emptiness of the first meaning.”
(The Great Nirvana Sutra)
[Rebirth and nirvana are but empty flowers on the wing]
Because both nirvana and birth and death are illusions (flowers in space). The Contemplation Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Birth and death and nirvana are like a dream of last night.”

Good people all, in practicing Chan one must be most careful. If this mountain monk had not be fallen ill at Chongqing, his life would almost have been wasted. What is essential is to meet a person of right knowledge and right view. Therefore the ancients sought instruction morning and evening, resolving body and mind, earnest and unremitting, to investigate this matter.”

[If this mountain monk had not fallen ill at Chongqing, his life would almost have been wasted] If I had not been critically ill and near death at Chongqing, and had personally been at that place, only then would I have known that intellectual understanding cannot overcome birth and death—my life would almost have been wasted. Having personally experienced that intellectual understanding cannot overcome birth and death, Dahui’s master, the Chan master Yuanwu Keqin, in his youth had the same experience. This is a warning bell for all cultivators.
The Continued Transmission of the Jewel of the Sangha records:
The Chan master Keqin studied under the patriarch Fayan of the Five Ancestors. “The teacher
(Keqin)
, relying on his eloquent argument, contested with him. Fayan was displeased
(Fayan was not pleased; yi means joy)
and said: ‘Can this overcome birth and death
(can your eloquence overcome birth and death)
? On a future day, when the lone lamp shines in the nirvana hall, you will test it yourself!’
(Keqin)
left because his views did not accord. When he reached Dinghui in Suzhou, he fell gravely ill and almost died. Then recalling his former investigations
(in the past)
, none were of any use
(at the moment of death, the earlier investigating practice was of no effect, and at the crux of birth and death he could not be master)
; only the old Fayan had not deceived me
(only the old teacher Fayan did not deceive me, but told me the truth: ‘Can this overcome birth and death?’)
. During his illness, that very day he packed his bundle and returned
(the moment the illness improved, that very day he packed and went back to Fayan)
. Fayan was glad he had come again, and accepted him as an attendant.
[Fayan of the Five Ancestors] In his later years the Chan master Fayan lived at the Eastern Chan Monastery on Wuzu Mountain in Qizhou, and was known by the world as “Fayan of the Five Ancestors.”
Only when you are intent, ponder at the place where thought cannot reach, and the mind has nowhere to go.”
Below are the instructions of the great patriarch Dahui, excerpted from the Recorded Sayings of the Chan Master Dahui Pujue:

A monk asked Zhaozhou: ‘Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?’ Zhaozhou said: ‘Wu.’ Only take the mind that idly thinks and turn it back upon the word ‘Wu’; try to think about it and see: suddenly, at the point where thought cannot reach, the moment this one thought breaks through, that is the place where you fully penetrate the three times.
Just this one
(Wu)

word is the knife that cuts off the road of birth and death. When a delusive thought arises, only lift the word ‘Wu’; lift it again and again, and then all at once news comes to an end—that is the secure resting place of returning home.

A thousand doubts, ten thousand doubts, are only one doubt. If the doubt on the hua-tou is broken, then a thousand and ten thousand doubts are broken at once; if the hua-tou is not broken, then on it you must struggle with it
(resist it)
. If you abandon the hua-tou, and instead raise doubt over other texts
(instead go fabricating delusions over texts)
, raise doubt over the scriptures and teachings, raise doubt over the gong-an of the ancients, raise doubt amid the toils of daily life—all of these are the family and followers of demons.
In the first place you must not take ownership at the place of lifting up, nor must you think and reckon,
only being intent to ponder at the place where thought cannot reach
, the mind having nowhere to go, a mouse entering the cow’s horn
(advancing without retreat)
, and then you will see the decisive conclusion
(then you will see the end results, pointing to seeing the nature and realizing the mind)
And again, if the heart
(mind)

is restless, only lift the topic ‘does a dog have Buddha-nature or not.’ Whether the words of the Buddha, the words of the patriarchs, or the words of the old masters of the various directions, diverging in a thousand ways—if you pass through that one word ‘Wu,’ you pass through them at once
(immediately pass through everything)
, so there is no need to ask anyone
(no need to ask others)
. If you keep
(if you are always)
asking others—how is the Buddha’s word, how is the patriarchs’ word, how is the old masters’ word—then throughout the aeons you will have no moment of enlightenment.
If the feeling of doubt has not broken, only contemplate a hua-tou by which an ancient entered the Way,
and move this mind that daily produces many delusions onto the hua-tou, then none of that conduct will proceed

. A monk asked Zhaozhou: ‘Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?’ Zhaozhou said: ‘Wu.’ Just this one word is the knife that cuts off the road of birth and death. When a delusive thought arises, only lift the word ‘Wu’; lift it again and again,
and all at once news comes to an end, which is the secure resting place of returning home
. There is nothing else extraordinary; the step forward spoken of before as hard to enter, unconcernedly you suddenly pass over it.

Constantly keep these two matters, ‘not knowing whence I was born, not knowing whither I will die,’ affixed to the very tip of your nose, and in tea and in meals, in stillness and in noise, thought after thought, diligent and unremitting
(thought after thought, diligent and tireless)
, constantly as though you owed a hundred thousand in cash, with no means to pay it
(unable to repay)
, heart vexed and oppressed, no door to escape
(unable to dodge the debt)
, unable to gain life, unable to seek death. At such a time
(at such a time)
, the paths of good and evil come one after another
(in succession)
to an end. When you feel it like this, just then is the time to apply strength; only look at a hua-tou right here.
[Such (
nèn
)] like this; thus.
A monk asked Zhaozhou: ‘Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?’ Zhaozhou said: ‘Wu.’ When looking at it, do not use measuring
(reckoning)

, do not use explication, do not need to get clear understanding, do not take ownership where the mouth opens, do not make a doctrine where it is lifted up, do not fall into the place of emptiness and stillness, do not use the mind to wait for enlightenment, do not grasp at the place where the masters speak, do not fall into the armor of doing nothing. Only in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, at all times lift and pull up ‘Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?’ ‘Wu.’ When the lifting becomes familiar, and mouth-discussion and mind-thought cannot reach, and within the heart it is in a turmoil, like biting a raw iron wedge with no flavor—at that time do not by any means retreat in will
(retreat in mind)
; when you are like this
(because you have reached such a state)
, it is a good sign.
[The armor of doing nothing] the shell of doing nothing at all, referring to an empty, still sitting with no delusions and also no investigation. The Chan master Fayan said:

“One must rouse one’s spirit vigorously, take up a hua-tou, investigate by day and investigate by night, and struggle on with it. Do not sit in the armor of doing nothing, nor sit to death on the meditation cushion. If deluded thoughts turn and multiply more and more, gently put it down, get off and take a walk, then take up the cushion again. Open both eyes, clench both fists, straighten the spine, and raise the hua-tou as before. Then you will feel the cool, like a cauldron of boiling water with a ladle of cold water scooped into it. Practicing thus, you will certainly reach the time of arriving home.” (From the Compendium of the Buddhas and Patriarchs)

Have you not heard the ancients’ saying: ‘The Buddha preached all dharmas to save all minds; if I have no mind at all, what need of all dharmas?’ It is not only so at the gate of the patriarchs; the entire great canon preached by the Buddha is all of this principle.

If the mind that doubts ‘not knowing whence I was born, not knowing whither I will die’ is not forgotten, then birth and death press together. Only at that pressed-together place, look at a hua-tou. A monk asked the Chan master Zhaozhou: ‘Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?’ Zhaozhou said: ‘Wu.’ Only take this mind that doubts ‘not knowing whence born, not knowing whither dying’ and move it onto the word ‘Wu’; then the pressed-together mind cannot proceed
(then the mind where birth and death press together cannot proceed)
. Since the pressed-together mind cannot proceed, then the mind that doubts birth and death coming and going will be near to ending.
Only at the place about to end but not yet ended, struggle on with it.
When the season and conditions arrive, all at once with a sudden spray it bursts apart, and then you accomplish what the teachings call
(then you attain what is in the scriptures and teachings)
‘putting an end to the mind of birth and death, stopping the mind of unwholesomeness, felling the thick forest of the mind, and washing the defilement of the mind.’

[Putting an end to the mind of birth and death, stopping the mind of unwholesomeness, felling the thick forest of the mind, and washing the defilement of the mind] Putting an end to the mind’s doubt and clinging toward birth and death, stopping the unwholesome thoughts in the mind, felling the thick forest of the mind (referring to the many varied thoughts), and washing the defilement of the mind (the karmic habits).

In walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, even in the rush and the fall, do not forget the meaning of the wondrous, pure, bright mind. When a delusive thought arises, there is no need to apply strength to dispel it; only lift: ‘A monk asked Zhaozhou: does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? Zhaozhou said: Wu.’ Lift it again and again, and there is not even the one lifting it to be seen; only this knowing that there is nothing to be seen is also not to be seen; then this phrase also has nothing to receive. All at once, at the place where there is nothing to receive, without realizing it you burst into a great laugh—at that very moment is the secure resting place of returning home.
Only constantly let the heart
(mind)

be empty and open, and with the mind of ‘not knowing whence born, not knowing whither dying,’ at all times lift it up at the place where you respond to conditions. When the lifting becomes familiar, after a long, long time it naturally becomes open and free
(the heart being empty and open)
. When you sense that daily activity is effortless
(when you sense that the lifting in daily activity is not at all laborious)
, that is the place where the study of this Way gains strength. At the place where you gain strength you save countless strength; at the place where you save strength, you gain countless strength.
Only do not, upon the words of the ancients, go on like stacking a pagoda, layer upon layer, wasting effort to no end. Only keep the mind in one place, and there is nothing unattained
(attained)
Sirs
(the assembly)

, if you can trust this mountain monk, try looking at the topic ‘does a dog have Buddha-nature or not’ in the midst of noise—not to speak of enlightenment or not. Just at the time when the heart is in turmoil, casually lift it up and consider: do you still sense stillness, do you still sense strength? If you sense strength, then do not let go. If you want to sit in stillness, only light a stick of incense and sit in stillness; while sitting do not let it sink into dullness, and do not let it be agitated. Dullness and agitation are what the sages reproved; when, in sitting stillness, you sense these two illnesses appear, only lift the topic ‘does a dog have Buddha-nature or not,’ and the two illnesses, without applying strength to dispel them, are right then tranquil
(a tamed, submissive appearance)
; as the days and months pass, only when you sense ease is it the place of gaining strength. Nor do you need to do the practice of stillness; just this
(lifting the topic ‘does a dog have Buddha-nature or not’)
is the practice.
[Tie tie
tiē tiē
] a still, quiet appearance; a tamed, submissive appearance.
[Agitation] the agitation of thoughts.
Only do not stir the mind to restrain and hold
(to bind and govern)
, but let the mind be forgotten; throughout the twelve hours let it be open and free. Suddenly an old habit flashes up
(suddenly springs up)

, and do not apply your heart to press it down; only at the place where it flashes up, look at a hua-tou: ‘does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? Wu.’ At just such a time, it is like a flake of snow upon a red-hot furnace
(the old habit melts away instantly)
[Giving instruction (fàng jiào)] to make; to cause.

Since he does not know whence he came, and does not know whither he goes, he feels his heart confused and stifled. When this very confusion arises, it is also nothing other; only look at a hua-tou right here. A monk asked Yunmen: ‘What is Buddha?’ Yunmen said: ‘A dried piece of shit.’ Only lift this saying, and suddenly, when all your tricks are exhausted, you will be enlightened.

By all means avoid seeking textual citations, or recklessly measuring and annotating. However clearly you annotate, however much you speak with a place to land on, it is all the business of ghosts. If the feeling of doubt is not broken, birth and death press together;

if the feeling of doubt is broken, then the mind of birth and death is ended. The mind of birth and death being ended, the views of buddha and the views of dharma are gone. If the views of buddha and dharma are still gone, how much more the arising of beings’ views of affliction?

Only take the mind of confusion and stifling and move it onto the dried piece of shit, pressing it firmly there. The mind that fears birth and death, the mind that is confused and stifled, the mind that thinks and discriminates, the mind that plays at being clever—all naturally cannot proceed. When you sense they do not proceed, do not fear falling into emptiness; suddenly, at the very place where you press it, news comes to an end, and you could not be more joyous in this whole life!

Once news is ended, to arouse the view of buddha, the view of dharma, the view of beings, to think, to discriminate, to play at being clever, to speak of doctrine—none of these obstruct. In the four forms of deportment in daily life, only always let it be open and free; in stillness and in noise, always lift the dried piece of shit; as days go and months come, the water-buffalo naturally grows tame. In the first place do not raise doubt elsewhere; when the doubt on the dried piece of shit is broken, then doubts as countless as the sands of the Ganges are broken at once.

[A dried piece of shit] that is, the bamboo chip for wiping; a small piece of bamboo or wood used to wipe away excrement. [The four forms of deportment] the rules of conduct that monks and nuns must observe, that is, being careful in the daily activities of rising and living, so as to maintain seriousness and dignity. The four forms of deportment are: walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. One should walk like the wind, stand like a pine, sit like a bell, and lie like a bow.
What is called practice is turning the mind that thinks of the dusty toils of the world onto the dried piece of shit,
causing emotion and discrimination not to proceed

, like a clay or wooden puppet. When you sense you are dull and have nothing to grasp hold of, that is a good sign. Do not fear falling into emptiness, nor think ahead and back about when you will attain enlightenment; if you keep such a mind, you fall into the wrong path. The Buddha says: ‘This dharma cannot be understood by thought or discrimination.’ To attach to it is to bring calamity.

[Grasp (bā bí)] a Chan-world term, also written as bā bí. Ba means to grasp, and bi refers to the ox’s nose; that is, threading a cord through the ox’s nose to control it. By extension it comes to mean a place one can get a grip on.
[To attach to it is to bring calamity] If you go to think and discriminate, then you will never attain enlightenment.
In daily life, at the place where you respond to conditions, the moment you sense yourself involved
(involved)

in differentiated states, only at that very differentiated place, lift the topic ‘does a dog have Buddha-nature or not.’ Do not make a thought of breaking through, do not make a thought of emotional dust, do not make a thought of differentiation, do not make a thought of the Buddha-dharma, but only look at the topic ‘does a dog have Buddha-nature or not.’ Only lift the word ‘Wu,’ and do not keep the mind waiting for enlightenment. If you keep the mind waiting for enlightenment, then the realm is differentiated, the Buddha-dharma is differentiated, the emotional dust is differentiated, the topic ‘does a dog have Buddha-nature or not’ is differentiated, the place of interruption is differentiated, the place of non-interruption is differentiated, the place where emotional dust deludes and disturbs body and mind and makes them uneasy is differentiated, and the one who can know so many differentiations is also differentiated. If you want to remove this illness, only look at the word ‘Wu.’
When lifting the topic, there is no need for so many tricks,
only in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down do not let it be interrupted

, and in joy and anger, sorrow and delight, do not give rise to discrimination. Lift it again and again, look at it again and again; when you feel there is no path, no flavor, and the heart hot and stifled, that is the place where this person must stake body and life. Remember! Remember! Do not, upon seeing such a state, retreat in mind; such a state is just the sign of becoming a buddha and a patriarch
(being)

Only take this mind of delusion and inversion, this mind of thinking and discriminating, this mind of loving life and hating death, this mind of views, knowledge, and understanding, this mind of delighting in stillness and disliking noise, and press them all down at once. Only at the place where you have pressed them down, look at a hua-tou—a monk asked Zhaozhou: ‘Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?’ Zhaozhou said: ‘Wu.’ This one word is the weapon
(weapon)
that destroys so many evil-knowing and evil-perceiving minds.

Do not take it as being or nonbeing, do not take it as a doctrine, do not think and reckon under the mind-organ, do not plant your root at the place of raising brows and blinking, do not ply your trade upon the path of words, do not fall into the armor of doing nothing, do not take ownership where it is lifted up, do not cite it in texts, but in the twelve hours and within the four forms of deportment, at all times lift it, at all times pull it up—‘does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? He said: Wu.’ Not apart from daily activities, try practicing like this and see; within a month or ten days
(a month or ten days)
you will see it for yourself.

Having bent your mind to investigate this great matter of the fundamental cause, since you have set this mind, in the first place do not be impatient; impatience makes it slower. Nor must you be slack; slackness makes it fall into neglect. Like the method of tuning the lute, tight and loose must be held in the mean, then the melody is achieved. Only in daily life, at the place of responding to conditions, at all times spy upon and catch: this
(of mine)
, this one who can decide right and wrong, crooked and straight for others—by whose grace and power? After all, from where does it flow? Spying and catching again and again,
the path of the formerly unfamiliar place naturally becomes familiar
(the road of what was formerly unfamiliar naturally becomes familiar)
; the unfamiliar
(investigating)
being familiar, then the familiar place becomes unfamiliar
Which
(which)

is the familiar place? The five skandhas, the six entries, the twelve places, the eighteen realms, the twenty-five existences, the ignorance and karmic consciousness, the mind-consciousness of thinking and calculating—shining day and night, like a wild horse never pausing—these are it. This whole chain
(this entire series)
makes beings wander in birth and death, makes beings do what is not good.
[Yi (
yi)

yi] bright and distinct in appearance; flickering in appearance.] [Five skandhas: also called the five aggregates, namely the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of thought, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness; these are the five great elements that constitute body and mind. Of these, the aggregate of form refers to matter and is called the ‘dharma of form’; the four aggregates of feeling, thought, formations, and consciousness belong to the mind and are called the ‘dharmas of mind.’ The aggregate of form is the body, while the other four aggregates (feeling, thought, formations, consciousness) are the mind. Master Yinguang says: “The five skandhas are form, feeling, thought, formations, and consciousness. Form is the body produced by the retribution of karma; feeling, thought, formations, and consciousness are the illusory, deluded mind that arises upon contact with objects. From this illusory body and mind, upon the six sense objects, one gives rise to confusion and creates karma.” (From the Essential Selections of Master Yinguang’s Writings.) The Nirvana Sutra says: “At the moment of death one’s relatives weep. The person is terrified and cannot control himself; the good and evil of his whole life all appear before him at once. After the warmth [of the body] is exhausted, the past five skandhas cease and the present intermediate being is born. After entering the womb, the present intermediate being ceases and the future five skandhas are born. It is like light arising as darkness ceases, and darkness arising as light ceases, continuing without a break.”] [Six entries: the six faculties entering the six objects is called ‘six entries,’ namely: eye enters form, ear enters sound, nose enters smell, tongue enters taste, body enters touch, and mind enters dharmas. The six entries are also another name for the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind).] [Twelve places and eighteen realms: the six faculties plus the six objects together are called the twelve places. ‘Place’ holds the meaning of arising, for from the six faculties and six objects the six consciousnesses arise. Thus the six faculties, six objects, and six consciousnesses together form the eighteen realms.] [Twenty-five existences: because fruits of existence are produced from karmic causes, the fruit is also called an ‘existence.’ The fruits of the three realms are divided into twenty-five categories, known as the twenty-five existences. Of these, the desire realm has fourteen existences, namely the four evil destinies (also called the four evil paths: hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras), the four continents (Eastern Purvavideha, Southern Jambudvipa, Western Godaniya, and Northern Uttarakuru), and the six desire heavens. The form realm has seven existences, namely the four dhyana heavens as four existences, and, in addition, the Great Brahma heaven, the five Pure Abode heavens, and the No-thought heaven as three existences. The formless realm has four existences, namely the four stations of emptiness.]
Once this entire chain has been born
(this whole series being then unfamiliar)
, then bodhi, nirvana, suchness, and Buddha-nature appear before one; and at the moment they appear there is also no measure to their appearing. Hence the ancient worthy
(Master Gaocheng)
having realized this, could say: ‘When responding to the eye, it is like a thousand suns
(like a thousand suns)

, and the ten thousand forms cannot escape its shadow and substance; when responding to the ear, it is like a deep valley, and great and small sounds alike are all fully [heard].’ Such things do not depend on seeking from another, do not borrow another’s power, but arise of themselves, vividly alive, in the place where one responds to conditions.
If you have not yet attained this, then turn this mind that ponders the dusty toils of the world back to the place where pondering cannot reach. Try to ponder it and see:
(which)

one is the place that pondering cannot reach? A monk asked Zhaozhou: “Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?” Zhaozhou said: ‘Wu’ (Not). Just this one word—whatever cleverness you have, please arrange it, please reckon it. When pondering, reckoning, and arranging leave no place to set them down, and you feel only a stifling in the belly and vexation in the heart, that is exactly the good season; the eighth consciousness is on the point of being brought to rest. When you feel it so, do not let go, but keep lifting and pulling on just this one word ‘Wu.’ Lift it and pull it again and again, and what was unfamiliar naturally becomes familiar, while what was familiar naturally becomes unfamiliar.

As long as emotional consciousness is not broken through, the heart-fire flickers on. At just such a moment, merely take up the topic of your doubt and keep hold of it. As when a monk asked Zhaozhou: “Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?” Zhaozhou said: ‘Wu.’ Just keep lifting it up and being aware of it. Coming from the left is not it, coming from the right is not it; nor may you seek to wait for enlightenment with the mind, nor claim it at the place where it is raised, nor take it as a mysterious comprehension, nor deliberate over it as existence or non-existence, nor conjecture it as the ‘no’ of a true nothing, nor sit within the shell of ‘nothing to do,’ nor grasp it at the place of striking fire from stone or a flash of lightning. When at last there is no mind to apply, and the mind has no place to rest, do not fear falling into emptiness—here is the good place. Suddenly, when a mouse enters a cow’s horn, you will see it broken off.

Continue only to lift and pull from time to time. When deluded thoughts arise, there is no need to check them with a stilling mind—just watch the huatou. Lifting while walking, lifting while sitting. Lift it and pull it, until it has no flavor; then is the good place, and one must not let go. Suddenly the flower of the mind blossoms and illumines the lands of the ten directions, and one can, upon the tip of a single hair, manifest the jewel-king lands, and, seated within a single particle of dust, turn the great Dharma-wheel.
